abstract: Guy Berger (Access/Macro, Guild, Burning Glass Institute) sets out a periodically updated list of his views on AI and the US labor market as of October 2026: no persistent mass unemployment, significant gross disruption, a very small average impact so far, and caution about reading aggregate data or confident forecasts.
keyFindings: Reasonably confident AI will not cause persistent mass unemployment, defined as something on the scale of 2009-13 or worse for a longer span.

Reasonably confident AI will cause significant gross labor-market disruption: rapid changes in the role and industry composition of employment, with declining wages and costly transitions for affected workers even if net effects are small.
Recessions and the business cycle remain the primary driver of aggregate unemployment; more disruption will happen within roles than across them.
AI's labor-market impact has on average been very small so far; larger in software development, yet software developers' share of US employment increased over the past year.
Aggregate indicators such as broad-industry employment counts are poor barometers of AI's impact; non-automation channels include uncertainty and a shift toward capital-intensive sectors.
AI is probably playing some role in higher unemployment for young college graduates but cannot explain the entire increase.
methodology: Expert judgment in a bulleted essay; no new data or estimates.
qualifiers: Opinion from a labor-market economist, explicitly not an AI specialist; claims are directional and unquantified. The author advises against trusting high-confidence predictions, including his own.
